title: Average selling price by category

brief.decision: Which categories to look at first in the price review, based on what customers really paid per unit in March 2025

expected_output.grain: one row per category that sold at least one unit in March 2025, Amsterdam time

checkpoints.prompt: Joost asks for the average selling price (ASP) of each category in a month: what customers paid per unit. Which calculation gives one category's ASP?

options.text: The average of the price paid per unit on each of the category's order lines, every line counted once
The category's total net revenue divided by the total number of units it sold
The category's total net revenue divided by the number of orders that included it
The average list price of the products in the category, taken from the product range

checkpoints.prompt: How many units did Voltmarkt sell in March 2025? An order counts for March 2025 when it was placed from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31, both days included, in Amsterdam time; order_ts holds the moment in UTC. Add up the units on every order line of those orders, in every category and channel. Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Joost's question.

Joost has a follow-up about Headphones. What percentage of the Headphones units Voltmarkt sold in March 2025 were sold with a promotion? An order counts for March 2025 when it was placed from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31, both days included, in Amsterdam time; order_ts holds the moment in UTC. An order line was sold with a promotion when its promo_id is not missing. Divide the units on those lines by all Headphones units sold that month and multiply by 100. Type the percentage with 1 decimal, for example 12.5.
Joost sees that the ASP of Headphones, what customers paid per unit, fell from February 2025 to March 2025. What can Joost conclude from that fall alone?

options.text: Voltmarkt cut its headphone list prices in March, so the new price list is working as planned
Fewer headphones were sold in March, and a lower number of units pulls the ASP down with it
Promotions or a shift to cheaper models can lower ASP with no list price change, so check those first
Headphone margins fell in March, because a lower ASP always means less profit on every unit

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Joost: what customers paid per unit across the categories in March 2025, which category stands out and why, one caveat, and one next step before Monday's price review.

model_plan:
Metric formula: ASP per category = total net revenue divided by total units, both summed over the month's order lines, not an average of line prices.
Output grain: one row per category that sold at least one unit in March 2025.
Tables and keys: sales (one row per order line) joined to orders on order_id for order_ts, and to products on product_id for category_id.
Filters: orders placed from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31 in Amsterdam time: convert order_ts from UTC to Amsterdam time first, then take the date.
Edge cases: orders late in the evening of 2025-02-28 UTC are already in March in Amsterdam, and late orders on 2025-03-31 UTC are already in April (the clocks move forward on 2025-03-30); promotion lines count at what customers paid; each line joins one order and one product, so nothing is counted twice.
Expected row count: 40
model_answer_template: In March 2025, {CP4} percent of the headphone units Voltmarkt sold carried a promotion from the Spring Audio Deals, most of them on a low-priced model, which pulled the Headphones ASP below February's. ASP mixes list prices, promotions and product mix, so a lower ASP does not mean the price list changed. Before Monday's review, I would set each category's March ASP next to its list price and its promotion share, starting with the audio categories.
follow_up_question: Which categories had a lower ASP in March than in February, and how much of each drop came from promotions?
